headline: Meta Just Open-Sourced an AI Agent That Beats Gemini's Little Brother — And It Runs on Your Gaming PC
summary: Meta's new Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter agentic model, is Apache 2.0 licensed and runs on a single consumer GPU, challenging proprietary AI models and their cost structures.
details: Meta has released Muse Glimmer, a 30-billion-parameter agentic model under an Apache 2.0 license. This model is quantized to under 20GB, allowing it to run on a single consumer GPU like an RTX 4090 or a 32GB MacBook without API keys or metering.

Muse Glimmer is distilled from Meta's flagship Muse Spark 1.2, designed specifically for agentic tasks such as tool calls, multi-step operations, and failure recovery. It aims to perform actions rather than just conversational chat.

While Muse Glimmer excels in general agentic reasoning and search, it doesn't win outright against all competitors. Alibaba's Qwen3.6-27B still outperforms it on terminal-heavy coding tasks, and Gemma4 shows superior safety metrics.

The model ships with day-one support for popular platforms like Ollama, LM Studio, Unsloth, llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM. Speculative decoding via Meta's "DFlash" drafter offers generation speeds up to 3.1x faster on an RTX 5090.

Mark Zuckerberg's accompanying essay, "The Future Is for Everyone," frames this release as a strategic move against closed-lab AI models. Meta aims to distribute capable models widely, challenging the concentration of superintelligence in a few proprietary systems.

Zuckerberg also defends distillation as a legitimate training method, addressing accusations that open labs merely leverage outputs from frontier closed models. This move is also a competitive response to the growing market share of Chinese open-weight labs.

The release coincides with OpenAI's 80% price cut for GPT-5.6 Luna, reducing it to $0.20 per million input tokens. This suggests a direct market response to the availability of powerful, free, open-source alternatives that can handle many common LLM tasks.

For developers building products that rely on LLM calls for tool use, routing, or agentic subtasks, Muse Glimmer offers a free and capable option that eliminates third-party API dependencies. Its Apache 2.0 license allows for commercial fine-tuning and deployment.

This release shifts the focus in AI from "whose model is smartest" to "who controls the meter that runs your product." Meta has effectively removed the metering cost for a significant range of use cases, forcing a reevaluation of existing AI budgets and strategies.

headline_marked: [[Two undersea cables reportedly damaged]] off Perth, Australia, following suspicious vessel activity
headline: Two undersea cables reportedly damaged off Perth, Australia, following suspicious vessel activity
summary: Two critical undersea internet cables off Perth have reportedly suffered shunt faults "straight after each other and in close proximity," coinciding with suspicious vessel activity in a protected zone. The Australian Federal Police are investigating.
details: Two of Australia's 16 critical undersea internet cables, carrying 99% of the nation's traffic, have reportedly been damaged off the coast of Perth. Subco CEO Bevan Slattery stated that two of his company's cables, Indigo-West and Indigo-Central, reported "shunt faults" in close succession and proximity.

The Indigo-West cable connects Perth to Indonesia and Singapore, while Indigo-Central links Victoria, Tasmania, and New South Wales. Slattery noted that the faults occurred around the same time a vessel was traversing the Submarine Cable Protection Zone off Perth.

A shunt fault indicates a broken conductor insulation, causing a short circuit. The incident happened within a Federally declared Cable Protection Zone, established in 2007, extending 51 nautical miles from shore at depths over 6,500 feet (2,000 meters).

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed they are investigating a report of a crime, hinting at potential sabotage. This incident follows a recent report from the National Security College highlighting growing threats to submarine cables globally.

Such incidents are not isolated; nation states have been suspected of cutting undersea infrastructure as part of "gray zone warfare." Finland has experienced similar disruptions, and Taiwan has increased naval patrols due to suspicious vessel activity near its cables.
